message.content:
HTTP status code **418** means **"I'm a teapot"** — and yes, it's a joke.

## The Background

It comes from **RFC 2324, "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)"**, published by the IETF on **April 1, 1998** (an April Fools' Day prank). The RFC describes a protocol for controlling coffee pots, and it includes this status code:

> **418 I'm a teapot**
> "Any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code '418 I'm a teapot'. The resulting entity body MAY be short and stout."

The last line is a nod to the nursery rhyme *"I'm a little teapot, short and stout."*

## In Practice

Despite being a joke, 418 has found real-world uses:

- **Anti-bot/anti-scraping measures** — some websites return 418 to suspicious requests
- **Playful API responses** — some services use it for fun or as a "you shouldn't be here" signal
- **Developer humor** — it's one of the most beloved jokes in the HTTP spec

## A Fun Fact

In 2017, there was some concern that 418 might be removed from HTTP status code registries. The developer community rallied behind it (the `save418.com` campaign appeared), and it was eventually preserved — it's now formally documented as a reserved status code in **RFC 9110** (HTTP Semantics), with the note:

> "This code was defined originally as part of an April Fools' joke... and it was expected that it would not be used by real HTTP servers. However, it has proven to be useful..."

So it went from April Fools' joke to an officially reserved, genuinely used status code. 🫖
